extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and critics interested in writing or evaluating heroic (verse) drama; educated readers of Restoration/epic-influenced theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing and judging 'heroic plays' — serious stage dramas in elevated verse that imitate the epic/heroic poem (focus on love and valour, spectacle, and heightened imagination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of elevated verse instead of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious plays of the heroic kind ought to be written in verse; they must not imitate ordinary conversation too nearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden: 'serious plays ought not to imitate conversation too nearly' — verse elevates thought and image beyond ordinary speech; while verse is harder to write well, it allows the poet to raise images and actions above common life. Anti-pattern: treating verse as mere ornament without corresponding elevated thought ('cozen[ing] many with their sound').

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate the heroic poem (in miniature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heroic play should be an imitation, in little, of an heroic poem — borrowing its scope, grandeur, and devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides structure and tone: the play should aim to reproduce epic majesty (gods, visions, grand incidents) on the stage; Dryden explicitly models heroic drama on Ariosto/Tasso/Virgil/Homer. Anti-pattern: treating a heroic play as merely a 'play in narration' without the fullness of an epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary subject: love and valour
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper subject-matter of an heroic play is love and valour (the combination typical of epic poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden cites Ariosto's program (Le donne, i cavalier, l'arme, gli amori) — love and courage should drive the action. Avoid making trivial or domestic matters the central concern when aiming for heroic dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: full plot and variety of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic drama should possess a well-filled design — a plenteous plot, variety of characters, and sufficient incidents to match the epic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden criticises earlier attempts for lacking 'fulness of a plot, and the variety of characters' — avoid sparse character lists or insufficient incident. The play should not feel thin or outline-like; it should provide varied persons and 'accidents' (events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of supernatural and visionary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectres, gods, magic, and visionary objects are permissible and often desirable in heroic poetry and plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden defends the use of ghosts and magic (Polydorus, Enchanted Wood, etc.) as essential beauties of epic-style writing; answers objections about improbability by noting historical and traditional belief in such things. Use them to heighten imagination, but ensure they serve poetic ends. Anti-pattern: excluding supernatural solely because it is 'unnatural' to modern taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle and stagecraft to raise the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of warlike instruments, battles, trumpets, drums, and visible spectacle is necessary to produce the effects of an heroic play and to persuade the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden: stage presentations of battle and sound effects aid the poet's aim of dominating spectators' minds; precedent given in Shakespeare and Jonson. Guidance: employ stagecraft where it contributes to imaginative effect rather than gratuitous show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for improbability for the sake of grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic plays are not strictly tied to probability or bare truth; a latitude for the marvelous and improbable is acceptable to achieve grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden: an heroic poet 'is not tied to a bare representation of what is true, or exceeding probable' — allowance for visionary/fantastic elements. Still, use improbability purposefully to serve poetry, not as careless nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic character may have eccentric virtues and flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero of an heroic play may be marked by extraordinary, even eccentric virtues (and faults) — a great spirit not wholly exempt from frailty makes for interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden: heroes may be 'not absolutely perfect, but of an excessive and over-boiling courage' — such imperfections ('moles and dimples') do not vitiate heroic beauty. Design heroic temperament (impatience, confidence, generosity) intentionally; avoid rendering flaws incoherent or incompatible with the hero's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere bombast — justify elevated or boastful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: While elevated diction and heroic boasting are part of the genre, excessive egoistic or nonsensical ranting undermines character and stage plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott criticises Almanzor's extravagant self-vaunting passages as 'rant' and examples are given; Dryden allows passion to broaden speech but warns against resulting nonsense. Ensure that grand speeches reveal character or plot-relevant emotion rather than empty bragging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion between lofty passages and measured thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain balance: combine moments of inflated heroic expression with 'less inflated' parts that convey just, ingenious, and beautiful ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott praises passages that show 'ideas ... as just, as ingenious and beautiful' amidst more inflated lines. Guidance: alternate grand rhetoric with clear, reasoned reflection to sustain readers' admiration without exhausting credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble balance — secondary characters should remain significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid casting every other person as a mere Lilliputian beside the hero; retain interest and plausible roles for secondary characters and subplots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott: 'The other personages of the drama sink into Lilliputians, beside the gigantic Almanzor' — maintain credible, interesting secondary characters and manage underplots so they are 'beautiful in themselves, and ingeniously managed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and plausibility of changes of fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes of fortune should not be so rapid as to destroy probability or reader/audience pleasure; preserve plausible tempo in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott: while rapid splendid events arrest attention, 'changes of fortune are too rapid to be either probable, or altogether pleasing.' Avoid accelerating incidents merely to amaze; respect narrative causality and audience expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations must be defensible and intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' motives (e.g., treachery, devotion, self-sacrifice) should be grounded in plausible emotional or cultural principles appropriate to the setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott notes Lyndaraxa's 'repeated and unparalleled treachery can only be justified by the extreme imbecility of her lovers' — an anti-pattern is to rely on weak characterization to excuse implausible acts. If using chivalric or romantic motives, make them coherent within the romance world portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchoring to locale and patriotic stakes when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the plot involves national or military peril, the play should evoke patriotism and local color rather than ignoring them entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott finds it a fault that, during a siege by religious/foreign enemies, 'the principle of patriotism is hardly once alluded to' — if context demands civic stakes, integrate them to give the drama fuller social/historical weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposeful use of supernatural apparitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparitions or ghosts onstage must have a clear dramatic purpose (character revelation, thematic reinforcement), not merely serve as ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott: the ghost of Almanzor's mother 'afforded an opportunity ... to throw in some fine poetry' but its professed purpose could have been trusted to other means; ensure ghosts advance characterization or plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical/epic precedents to justify stylistic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify departures from realism by appeal to epic precedent (Homer, Virgil, Tasso, Ariosto) — gods, visions, and grand devices have illustrious models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden repeatedly references epic authors as authority for using the marvelous and for heroic excess. This is both a defense and stylistic guide: refer to epic examples to structure and ornament the play appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage persuasion: aim for dominion over spectators' minds
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet-playwright should strive to dominate the spectators' imagination, using language, incident, and stage means to persuade them that what they behold is happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden: 'The poet is then to endeavour an absolute dominion over the minds of the spectators' — use all available dramatic arts (music, sound, spectacle, diction) to secure imaginative immersion. Anti-pattern: leaving the audience unconvinced because of inadequate theatrical means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the unity of heroic tone — avoid hybrid confusions
rubrics_metrics.description: If adopting the heroic-epic mode, avoid inconsistent mixes of low comedy or purely conversational prose that undermine the heroic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden defends the distinctiveness of heroic verse and the need to sustain its elevated style; while some prose may be mixed, a consistent heroic plan and tone is necessary for the audience to accept the genre's premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sound and musical recitative where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitative music and heightened musical elements (derived from earlier operatic practices) can legitimately be used to support the heroic style onstage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden notes Sir William D'Avenant's use of recitative music and Italian opera devices as precedents; musical presentation may assist in raising passion and grandeur. Use music to underscore—not replace—poetic substance.
